# NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Password Length Requirements

## 1. Source resolution (do this before quoting any number)

"63B-4" resolves to **NIST SP 800-63B, Revision 4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management** — the final published revision in the SP 800-63-4 suite. The governing text is **Sec. 3.1.1.2, "Password Verifiers"**, which sits inside Sec. 3, whose preamble states: *"This section is normative... the technical requirements for each authenticator type are the same, regardless of the AAL at which the authenticator is used."*

**Critical disambiguation — do not answer from the draft.** Two different number sets circulate under the "800-63B-4" label:

| Source | Text | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **NIST SP 800-63B-4 (final)**, Sec. 3.1.1.2 items 1–2 | Single-factor **SHALL** ≥ 15; MFA-only **MAY** be shorter but **SHALL** ≥ 8; **SHOULD** permit max ≥ 64 | **Authoritative — the answer** |
| NIST SP 800-63B-4 **2pd** (August 2024 second public draft), Sec. 3.1.1.2 items 1–2 | **SHALL** ≥ 8 and **SHOULD** ≥ 15; **SHOULD** permit max ≥ 64 | **Superseded draft — do NOT quote** |

The draft collapsed both cases into a single 8-char SHALL / 15-char SHOULD. The final text splits them and promotes both to SHALL. Answering "8 for single-factor" or "15 as a SHOULD" is an error against the final document.

## 2. The three answers

| # | Question | Value | Normative force | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum length verifiers **must require** for a password used as a **single-factor** authentication mechanism | **15 characters** | **SHALL** (mandatory) | SP 800-63B-4, Sec. 3.1.1.2, item 1 |
| 2 | Minimum length for a password used **only as part of multi-factor authentication** | **8 characters** | **SHALL** (mandatory floor); verifiers **MAY** allow shorter than 15 in this case | SP 800-63B-4, Sec. 3.1.1.2, item 1 |
| 3 | Maximum length verifiers **should permit at least** | **64 characters** | **SHOULD** (recommendation, not a SHALL) | SP 800-63B-4, Sec. 3.1.1.2, item 2 |

Verbatim normative text (Sec. 3.1.1.2, items 1–2):

> 1. Verifiers and CSPs **SHALL** require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length. Verifiers and CSPs **MAY** allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but **SHALL** require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length.
>
> 2. Verifiers and CSPs **SHOULD** permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters.

Corroboration, NIST SP 800-63-4 Implementation Resources FAQ (SP 800-63B section): *"Minimum password length of 15 characters for passwords being used as a single authentication factor at AAL1 (increased from 8 characters)."*

### Notes that prevent misreads
- **Not AAL-dependent.** Per the Sec. 3 preamble, the 15/8/64 requirements apply identically at AAL1, AAL2, and AAL3. There is no AAL1-vs-AAL3 password-length table to consult.
- **"8" is a floor, not a target.** The MFA case permits shorter than 15 but never shorter than 8; a verifier that requires 15 everywhere is compliant (it satisfies both SHALLs).
- **Do not confuse with activation secrets.** Sec. 3.1.1.2 governs *centrally verified* passwords. Locally verified **activation secrets** for multi-factor authenticators are a separate construct with a 4-character minimum (6 encouraged) per the FAQ and the activation-factor requirements — those are **not** "passwords used as part of MFA" in the sense of ask 2. Answering 4 to ask 2 is wrong.
- **"64" is a SHOULD.** It is a floor on the maximum the verifier permits, i.e. the verifier must not reject a 64-character password. NIST's rationale (Appendix A) is that hash output size is independent of input length, so long passphrases should be allowed; only pathologically long inputs (megabytes) justify a cap.

## 3. Implementation requirements that ride along with these numbers

A verifier that hard-codes 15/8/64 but violates the surrounding items is non-compliant. The same section requires:

1. **Count Unicode code points, not bytes or UTF-16 units.** Item 4: *"Each Unicode code point **SHALL** be counted as a single character when evaluating password length."* So `"pässwörd-🔑-long"` length = code-point count. Normalize (NFC) before counting so canonical-equivalent inputs are measured consistently, and count **before** any hashing.
2. **Accept printing ASCII + space (SHOULD)** and **Unicode (SHOULD)** — do not reject non-ASCII or embedded spaces.
3. **No composition rules (SHALL NOT)** — no "must contain upper/lower/digit/symbol" checks (item 5).
4. **No periodic rotation (SHALL NOT)** — never force password changes on a schedule (item 6).
5. **No truncation.** If the verifier caps length, the cap must be ≥ 64 and must be enforced by *rejecting* an over-long password at enrollment with a clear error — never by silently truncating (truncation collapses distinct passwords and breaks the code-point-counting requirement).
6. **Blocklist on choice/change (SHALL).** Chosen passwords must be checked against a blocklist of commonly used, expected, or compromised values; a rejected subscriber must be required to choose a different one. This is what replaces composition rules as the strength control.
7. **Allow password managers / autofill / paste** (per FAQ) — no `autocomplete="off"` on the password field, no blocking paste.
8. **Salt ≥ 32 bits, unique per account; store salt + hash; approved hashing scheme** (e.g. PBKDF2 per SP 800-132 with a current work factor, or a memory-hard scheme per updated NIST guidance); optionally a verifier-held pepper stored separately in a hardware-protected area.

## 4. Reference verifier logic (language-neutral, then pseudocode)

Configuration contract — encode the three numbers as explicit, separately-sourced fields so the single-factor and MFA cases cannot drift into one another:

```json
{
  "passwordPolicy": {
    "singleFactor": { "minLength": 15, "source": "SP800-63B-4 3.1.1.2#1" },
    "mfaOnly":      { "minLength": 8,  "source": "SP800-63B-4 3.1.1.2#1" },
    "maxLengthPermitted": 64,
    "maxLengthPermittedSource": "SP800-63B-4 3.1.1.2#2 (SHOULD)",
    "countUnit": "unicode_code_points_nfc",
    "compositionRules": [],
    "periodicRotationDays": null,
    "truncate": false
  }
}
```

Validation procedure on password **choice/change**:

```
function validateNewPassword(raw, context):   # context = SINGLE_FACTOR | MFA_ONLY
    s = unicodeNFC(raw)
    if containsNUL_or_controlCharsOtherThanTab(s): reject("invalid characters")
    n = codePointCount(s)                       # NOT bytes, NOT UTF-16 units

    minRequired = (context == SINGLE_FACTOR) ? 15 : 8
    if n < minRequired:
        reject("password must be at least " + minRequired + " characters")

    if n > MAX_PERMITTED:                       # MAX_PERMITTED >= 64, e.g. 64 or 256
        reject("password must be at most " + MAX_PERMITTED + " characters")
        # reject, never truncate

    if isOnBlocklist(s):                        # compromised/common/expected
        reject("password is too common or has appeared in a breach; choose another")

    # NO composition checks. NO rotation scheduling.
    storeSaltAndHash(s)                         # salt >= 32 bits, unique per account
    return accept

function validateLoginAttempt(raw, context):
    # Same length bounds applied for early rejection; hash comparison is constant-time.
    # Rate-limit per account and per IP; this is the primary online-guessing control.
```

**MAX_PERMITTED choice:** set it to 64 (the NIST floor on the maximum) or higher — 64, 128, or 256 are all compliant. Anything below 64 violates the SHOULD in item 2. If you pick a value above 64, also cap the request body / hash input size at the transport layer (e.g. 1 KiB) so a multi-megabyte submission cannot be used as a CPU-exhaustion vector, and surface the cap as a 400 with the actual limit.

## 5. Test vectors for the acceptance suite

| Input | Context | Code points | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"Tr0ub4dor&3xy"` (14 chars) | SINGLE_FACTOR | 14 | **reject** (below 15) |
| `"correct horse battery staple"` (28 chars, spaces) | SINGLE_FACTOR | 28 | **accept** (spaces allowed; no composition rule applies) |
| `"Tr0ub4dor&3xy"` (14 chars) | MFA_ONLY | 14 | **accept** (≥ 8) |
| `"abcd1234"` (8 chars) | MFA_ONLY | 8 | **accept** (exactly at floor) |
| `"abcd123"` (7 chars) | MFA_ONLY | 7 | **reject** (below 8) |
| 64-char ASCII string | any | 64 | **accept** (must not be rejected) |
| 65-char string, MAX_PERMITTED=64 | any | 65 | **reject** with explicit over-length error, **not truncated** |
| `"pässwörd-🔑-aaaaaaaa"` | SINGLE_FACTOR | 20 | **accept** (code points, not bytes: 24 bytes) |
| `"password"` | any | 8 | **reject** (blocklist) — even though it is 8 chars and would pass MFA length |
| `"Ab1!"` | any | 4 | **reject** in both contexts (4 is the activation-secret floor, not a password floor) |

## 6. Answer, condensed

- **Single-factor password minimum: 15 characters (SHALL).**
- **Password used only as part of MFA minimum: 8 characters (SHALL; shorter than 15 permitted, never below 8).**
- **Maximum length verifiers should permit at least: 64 characters (SHOULD).**

All three from NIST SP 800-63B-4 (final), Sec. 3.1.1.2 "Password Verifiers," items 1 and 2; lengths measured in Unicode code points.
